The value <number of hugepages> can be computed by taking the amount of memory we want to devote to VMs, and dividing it by the page size (1 GiB). For example on our host with 2 TiB of RAM, creating 1792 Huge Pages means we can accommodate up to 1792 GiB of VMs’ RAM, and leave plenty (~214 GiB) to the host OS.

sect2.title: Automatic NUMA balancing
sect2.para: NUMAB can be useful in dynamic virtualization scenarios, where VMs are created, destroyed and re-created relatively quickly. Or, in general, it can be useful in cases where it is not possible or desirable to statically partition the host resources and assign them explicitly to VMs. This, however, comes at the price of some latency being introduced. Plus, NUMAB’s own operation can interfere with VMs’ execution and cause further performance degradation. In any case, this document focuses on achieving the best possible performance for VMs, through specific tuning and static resource allocation, therefore it is recommended to leave NUMAB turned off. sect2.title: Services, daemons and power management
sect2.para: Service daemons have been discussed already, in the first part of the document. Most of the considerations made there apply here as well.

For example, tuned should either not be used, or the profile should be set to one that does not implicitly put the CPUs in polling mode. Both throughput-performance and virtual-host profiles from SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 are okay, as neither of them touches /dev/cpu_dma_latency.

irqbalance can be a source of latency, for no significant performance improvement. The suggestion is again to disable it for latency sensitive workloads. This means, though, that IRQs may need to be manually bound to the appropriate CPUs, considering the IO topology.
As far as power management is concerned, the cpufreq governor can either be kept as it is by default, or switched to performance, depending on the nature of the workloads of interest.

note.title: Power management
note.para: For anything that concerns power management, changing the tuned profile or using cpupower, from the host OS will have the effects one can expect, and described already in the first half of the document.

sect2.title: Confidential Computing Technologies (SEV-SNP)
sect2.para: Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) technology is available on the 6th Generation AMD EPYC Processors and supported on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1. It allows the memory of the VMs to be encrypted, enabling a high level of confidentiality. SEV-SNP builds on top of SEV with Encrypted State (SEV-ES), since CPU registers are also encrypted when they are saved into the host memory, and it also guarantees (among other things) the integrity of the VM. For using SEV-SNP for a VM, we need to enable it in the VM’s own configuration file, but there are preparation steps that need to occur at the host level.

The libvirt documentation contains all the necessary steps required for enabling SEV-SNP on a host that supports it. It has been enough to add the following boot parameters to the host kernel command line, in the boot loader:
For further details, refer to libvirt documentation: Enabling SEV on the host.
All the experiments described in this document, including the ones on the host and in the VMs that do not use memory encryption, were run with the host configured as described above.
What happens when SEV-SNP is used for encrypting VMs' memory is described later in the guide.

sect1.title: Resource allocation and tuning of VMs
sect1.para: For instructions on how to create an initial VM configuration, start the VM, and install a guest OS, refer to the SUSE documentation at Managing Virtualization Platforms with libvirt (section Guest installation).
From a VM configuration perspective, the two most important factors for achieving top performance on CPU and memory bound workloads are:

listitem.para: Partitioning of host resources and placement of the VMs
Enlightenment of the VMs about their virtual topology

sect1.para: For example, if there are two VMs, each one should be run on one socket, to minimize CPU contention and maximize memory access parallelism. Also, and especially if the VMs are big enough, they should be made aware of their own virtual topology. That way, all the tuning actions described in the first part of this document become applicable to the workloads running inside the VMs too.

sect2.title: Placement of VMs
sect2.para: When a VM is created, memory is allocated on the host to act as its virtual RAM. Moving this memory, for example on a different NUMA node from the one where it is first allocated, incurs (when possible) a significant performance impact. Therefore, it is of paramount importance that the initial placement of the VMs is as optimal as possible. KVM can make educated guesses on what a good placement might be. For the purpose of this document, however, we are interested in what is the absolute best possible initial placement of the VMs, taking into account the specific characteristics of AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processor systems. And this can only be achieved by manually doing the initial placement. Of course, this comes at the price of reduced flexibility, and is only possible when there is no oversubscription.

Deciding on what pCPUs the vCPUs of a VM run, can be done at creation time, but also easily changed along the VM lifecycle. It is, however, still recommended to start the VMs with good vCPUs placement.
Placement of VM memory on host NUMA nodes happens by means of the <numatune> XML element:
sect2.screen: <numatune> <memory mode='strict' nodeset='0-1'/> <memnode cellid='0' mode='strict' nodeset='0'/> <memnode cellid='1' mode='strict' nodeset='1'/> ... </numatune>
sect2.para: The 'strict' guarantees that all the memory for the VM will come only from the (set of) NUMA node(s) specified in nodeset. A cell is, in fact, a virtual NUMA node, with cellid being its ID and nodeset telling exactly from what host physical NUMA node(s) the memory for this virtual node should be allocated.

The correctness of this kind of tuning can be verified checking on which NUMA node(s) the memory of the QEMU processes representing the VMs have been allocated on, by using the numastat tool (on the host) like this:
In fact, we see that there is only 1 QEMU process (as there is only 1 VM running) and its memory footprint has been equally split between the two NUMA nodes.
A NUMA-unaware VM can still include this element in its configuration file. It will have only one <memnode> element, and the output of numastat will look like this:

In this case there are 2 VMs running and their memory has been pretty much entirely allocated on a single NUMA node: Node 0 for the VM associated to the QEMU process with PID 215841, and Node 1 for the other one.
A similar, but more complex example is also shown below. There are sixteen VMs, and they have been evenly distributed between the two nodes:
Placement of vCPUs happens via the <cputune> element, as in the example below:
sect2.screen: <vcpu placement='static'>1024</vcpu> <cputune> <vcpupin vcpu="0" cpuset="0"/> <vcpupin vcpu="1" cpuset="512"/> <vcpupin vcpu="2" cpuset="1"/> <vcpupin vcpu="3" cpuset="513"/> ... <vcpupin vcpu="512" cpuset="256"/> <vcpupin vcpu="513" cpuset="768"/> <vcpupin vcpu="514" cpuset="257"/> <vcpupin vcpu="515" cpuset="769"/> ... </cputune>
sect2.para: The value 1024 means that the VM has 1024 vCPUs. static guarantees that each vCPU will stay on the pCPU(s) it is pinned to. The various <vcpupin> elements are where the mapping between vCPUs and pCPUs is established (vcpu being the vCPU ID and cpuset being either one or a list of pCPU IDs).
To be able to create VMs with more than 255 vCPUs, the following element should be added in the <devices> section:

In fact, QEMU uses a static SMT sibling CPU ID assignment. This is how we guarantee that virtual SMT siblings will always execute on actual physical SMT siblings:

The following sections give more specific and precise details about placement of vCPUs and memory for VMs of varying sizes, on the reference system for this guide (see ). Note that we can actually create VMs as large as our test host is, that means a VM with 1024 virtual CPUs (which is, however, beyond the maximum number of vCPUs per VM that is officially supported on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, that is 768, see Virtualization Support in SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, section KVM limits).

sect3.title: Placement of a single large VM
sect3.para: An interesting use case is when only one VM is used. Reasons for doing something like that include security/isolation, flexibility, high availability, and others. In these cases, typically, the VM is almost as large as the host itself.
Let us, therefore, consider a VM with 1024 vCPUs and 1792 GiB of RAM. Such a VM spans multiple host NUMA nodes and therefore it is recommended to create a virtual NUMA topology for it.

We should create a virtual topology with 2 virtual NUMA nodes (that is, as many as there are physical NUMA nodes), and split the VM’s memory equally among them. The 1024 vCPUs are assigned to the 2 nodes, 512 on each. This way, if a suitable virtual topology is also provided to the VM, each of the VM’s vCPUs will access its own memory directly, and use Infinity Fabric inter-socket links only to reach foreign memory, as it happens on the host. Workloads running inside the VM can be tuned exactly like they were running on a bare metal 6th Generation AMD EPYC Processor server.
The following example numactl output comes from a VM configured as explained:

This is analogous to the host topology, also from the point of view of NUMA node distances (as the libvirt version present in SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 allows us to define the virtual nodes distance table). The only differences are the CPU IDs (the two SMT threads of each core have adjacent IDs in the VM, while on the host they are 512 apart) and the amount of memory.
See for a complete VM configuration file.

As said already, full cores must always be used. If possible always fully use CCXes/dies too. Since each die has 64 CPUs, that means that a VM with 1024 vCPUs will use all the 8 CCXes, on each of the 2 nodes (as 8 x 64 x 2 is indeed 1024). So, for example, vCPUs 0 to 63 can be assigned to Cores L#0 to L#31 (and hence to CPUs P#0 to P#31 and P#512 to P#543), on node P#0; vCPUs 64 to 127 to Cores L#32 to L#63, and so on (and the same on node P#1). In fact, this is what we call coherent 1-to-1 mapping between virtual and physical topologies.

sect3.title: Placement of two large VMs
sect3.para: If wanting to run two VMs, they both can have 512 vCPUs and 896 GiB memory each. Therefore, each one can fit in one of the host's NUMA nodes. This also means that there is no need to define virtual NUMA nodes in their configuration.
Placing each VM on one node means that workloads running inside each of them will never need to use inter-socket interconnect.
In this example scenario, numactl output of both VMs looks as follows:

sect3.title: Placement of four to sixty-four medium-size VMs
sect3.para: Following the same principles, we can split each node in 2, and have 4 VMs with 256 vCPUs and up to 448 GiB of RAM each. It is also feasible to have 8 VMs with 128 vCPUs and up to 224 GiB of RAM each, 16 VMs with 64 vCPUs and 112 GiB RAM, 32 VMs with 32 vCPUs and 56 GiB RAM, or even 64 VMs, all with 16 vCPUs and 28 GiB RAM.

In the first case, each VM will span 4 host dies. In the second and in the third cases, 2 and 1 dies. And in the fourth and fifth ones, each VM will be pinned to half and a quarter of a die, respectively.

In all these situations, VMs do not need to (and, therefore, should not) be placed across the host NUMA nodes boundary, and hence they do not need to be NUMA-aware. They still benefit from having a virtual topology, in terms of cores, threads and dies which matches the resource they are using (discussed in more detail in the following section).

sect3.title: Placement of many small VMs
sect3.para: If small VMs are the target, VMs with either 8, 4 or 2 vCPUs each can be created and efficiently allocated on AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processors servers.

VMs with 8 vCPUs occupy an eighth of a die, and we can have 128 of them. VMs with either 4 or 2 vCPUs will be given 2 and 1 host cores and we can have 256 and 512 of them, respectively. And this is all possible without the need for any of the VMs to span more than one host NUMA node.

Of course, in all these cases, VMs are sharing dies, which means VMs will interfere with each other via the L3 caches. This may or may not be a problem, but there is no way around it, as soon as more VMs than the number of available dies are necessary. The performance impact of such sharing should be tolerable, in most cases, for these configurations, but this needs to be assessed with tests and benchmarks. If that is not the case, then the recommendation is to not go above 16 VMs. More clever (but also more complex) tuning strategies can be designed, but they would require further a-priori knowledge of the workload and/or the load profile of the various VMs, which may not be always available (or can change during the lifecycle of the VMs).

note.title: Hundreds of VMs with limited RAM size and disk space
note.para: When the number of VMs increases so much, the limiting factor will become the memory or the disk. With ~1800 GiB of RAM available for VMs on our server, we can give only 3 GiB of RAM to each of the 512 VMs of the last example above. Of course, this limitation is only an issue of the system used as reference for this guide. The AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processor architecture itself can accommodate much more RAM.

sect3.para: In cases when it is enough or desirable to have VMs with only 1 vCPU, it is recommended to still not go beyond 512, and assign no less than one full core to each VM. In fact, it should be avoided to have vCPUs from different VMs running on two sibling threads of the same core. Such a solution, although functional, is not ideal for all the cases where good and consistent performance within VMs is a goal (as well as for security concerns, but that is out of the scope of this guide). What can be done for each VM and for each core is to use one of the two threads for the actual vCPU, and the other for its IO thread(s), on the host. This solution allows taking advantage of the full 6th Generation AMD EPYC processing power. However, we advise to check and verify whether this is a good setup and if it brings performance benefits for the specific workloads of interest, before committing to it.

sect2.title: Emulator IO threads
sect2.para: IO for the VMs is carried out by device emulators running on the host, or by the so-called back-ends of paravirtualized drivers (also running on the host). Both the IO threads of the emulators and the back-ends are seen as (either user or kernel) threads by the host OS. As such, they can be configured to run on specific subsets of the CPUs assigned to the host OS. And their placement on such CPUs may have an impact on performance of VMs, especially on IO bound workloads.

For example, a 1 vCPU VM can have its vCPU bound to the one SMT thread of a core, while the other thread can be assigned to the host, and the IO thread(s) of the VM pinned to it. The idea behind this is that a common execution pattern for the vCPU is to be idle when the IO threads are busy. Hence this setup potentially maximizes the exploitation of hardware resources.

sect2.title: Oversubscription of host resources
sect2.para: Oversubscription happens when the demand for some resource is higher than what is physically available. In virtualization, this can happen for CPU and memory.

note.title: Not covering oversubscribed scenarios
note.para: This guide does not cover oversubscribed scenarios in great detail. However, given the large number of CPUs available on an AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processor system and the huge amount of memory the architecture supports, this is not considered a limitation.

sect2.para: CPU oversubscription happens when the total cumulative number of vCPUs from all VMs becomes higher than 1024. Such a situation inevitably introduces latencies, resulting in lower performance compared to when host resources are sufficient. It is, however, impossible to tell a priori to what extent this happens, at least not without a detailed knowledge of the actual workload.

If we knew in advance that the load on each vCPU will always stay below 50%, we could assume that even oversubscribing the host by a factor of 2 (like with ~2048 vCPUs in total, in our case!) will work well. On the other hand, if we knew that the load that each vCPU tries to impose on the system is always 100%, creating even 1 vCPU more than the host has pCPUs can be considered a misconfiguration.

When oversubscription is necessary, exclusive 1-to-1 vCPU to pCPU assignment may not be the best approach and we need to trust the hypervisor scheduler to handle the situation well. What can be done, though, is providing such scheduler at least with some suggestions, if we have enough knowledge about the workload. For example, we can try to help the scheduler avoid that all the VMs running CPU intensive workloads end up on the same nodes, or avoid cross-node VM migrations happening too frequently.

This grouping of VMs on (a set of) nodes can be done with some less strict forms of vCPU pinning (often called affinity), or with other mechanisms. For example, cgroups can be leveraged on a KVM host.

Memory oversubscription happens when the total cumulative amount of memory used by all VMs is more than the RAM available on the host. In this case, some of that memory is kept outside of the RAM (swapped out) when the VMs using it are not running. It is put back in RAM (swapped in) when these VMs run again. This also has (potentially severe) performance implications, and is not analyzed in detail here.
Swapping is handled by Linux virtual memory management and paging code and mechanism, exactly as it happens for host/bare metal processes.
Then there are page sharing and memory ballooning.

Page sharing relies on the principle that, when VMs use memory pages which are identical, only one copy of them needs to be kept in physical RAM, at least for most of the time. This is supported on KVM, via a mechanism called Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM).

Ballooning relies on the idea that VMs do not always use all the memory they are configured to be able to use. This is supported in KVM. However, using it is not ideal for performance, thus it is not analyzed in any further detail in this document.
This is always considered a misconfiguration. In fact:

listitem.para: A single VM should never have more vCPUs than the host has pCPUs.
A single VM should never have more memory than the host has physical RAM.

sect2.title: Enlightenment of VMs
sect2.para: The term enlightenment refers to letting the guest OS know as many details as possible about the virtual topology of the VM. This is only useful and brings actual performance improvements only if such topology is properly and effectively mapped on host resources, and if such mapping is stable and does not change during the life of the VM.

sect3.title: Virtual CPUs model and topology
sect3.para: To ensure the VM has a vCPU topology, use the following:
sect3.screen: <cpu mode="host-model" check="none"> <topology sockets="2" dies="8" cores="32" threads="2"/> <numa> <cell id="0" cpus="0-511" memory="939524096" unit="KiB"> <distances> <sibling id="0" value="10"/> <sibling id="1" value="32"/> </distances> </cell> <cell id="1" cpus="512-1023" memory="939524096" unit="KiB"> <distances> <sibling id="0" value="32"/> <sibling id="1" value="10"/> </distances> </cell> </numa> </cpu>
sect3.para: The <topology> element specifies the CPU characteristics. In this case, we are creating vCPUs which will be seen by the guest OS as being arranged in 2 sockets, each of which has 8 dies, each of which has 32 cores with 2 threads (that is 64 CPUs). And this is how we match, for the one big VM, the topology of the host.

Each <cell> element defines one virtual NUMA node, specifying how much memory and which vCPUs are part of it. The <distances> elements allow us to define a custom virtual NUMA distance table. Values should be - as it is on actual hardware - an indication of the latency of accessing the memory of every node from any other. And again we are defining a virtual distance table which exactly matches the host one, for the one big VM.

CPU model is how the VM is told what type of vCPUs should be emulated, for example, what features and special instructions and extensions will be available. To achieve best performance, using model='host-passthrough' is often the right choice. However, at least on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, this produces wrong results. In fact, such setting prevents the topology - despite it being described correctly in the <topology> element - from being interpreted correctly, inside the VM. This is visible in the output of the command lscpu:
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # lscpu ... CPU(s): 1024 On-line CPU(s) list: 0-1023 Vendor ID: AuthenticAMD Model name: AMD EPYC 9996 256-Core Processor CPU family: 26 Model: 81 Thread(s) per core: 1 Core(s) per socket: 512 Socket(s): 2 ... L1d cache: 64 MiB (1024 instances) L1i cache: 64 MiB (1024 instances) L2 cache: 512 MiB (1024 instances) L3 cache: 16 GiB (1024 instances) ...
sect3.para: Both the CPU topology and the cache layout, as seen from inside of the VM, are completely wrong, and can affect performance of applications running inside the VM. In fact, not only the sizes of the various cache levels are wrong. It is also the information about which CPUs share what caches that is completely misconfigured, as shown also here:
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/shared_cpu_list 0 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index1/shared_cpu_list 0 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index2/shared_cpu_list 0 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index3/shared_cpu_list 0-511
sect3.para: The VM thinks that L1d, L1i and L2 are private of each vCPU, while that is not the case, as they are shared by the two threads of each core. Even worse, it thinks that L3 is shared across all the vCPUs of a socket, which is not true, as it is shared only among 32 cores (that is 64 vCPUs).

For this reason, the recommendation is to use EPYC-Turin as the CPU model (as an appropriate model for 6th Generation AMD EPYC Processors (codename Venice) is not yet available in the QEMU and libvirt of SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1) either manually or by using model='host-model'. This enables a virtual topology inside the VM that is more consistent (although not perfectly identical) with the one of the host, and benchmarks show a beneficial effect on performance coming from that. The output of lscpu with EPYC-Turin as a model is shown below:
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # lscpu ... CPU(s): 1024 On-line CPU(s) list: 0-1023 Vendor ID: AuthenticAMD Model name: AMD EPYC-Turin Processor CPU family: 26 Model: 0 Thread(s) per core: 2 Core(s) per socket: 256 Socket(s): 2 ... L1d cache: 24 MiB (512 instances) L1i cache: 16 MiB (512 instances) L2 cache: 512 MiB (512 instances) L3 cache: 512 MiB (16 instances) ...
sect3.para: Of course, now it is the Model name: that is not completely correct. But both the CPU and caches layout is much more in line with what we wanted to achieve by tuning the VM configuration.

In fact, the L3 cache size is off, with regard to the host value (512 MiB instead of 2 GiB). And this is because it is the value taken from previous generation AMD EPYC Processors architecture characteristics. But the cache topology and cache level sharing among vCPUs are now correct (as shown below). And this is far more important for achieving good performance inside the VM.
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index1/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index2/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index3/shared_cpu_list 0-63
sect3.para: Note that, to achieve the outcome shown above, it is very important to use the following CPU topology description string, in the VM configuration:

In particular, do not omit the dies="8" element, as that is what enables the VM to see its vCPUs grouped in dies (the CCXes of the host). In fact, using something like this <topology sockets="2" cores="256" threads="2"/> would result in a correct CPU topology, but the representation of the cache layout would still be inaccurate, such as:
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # lscpu ... CPU(s): 1024 On-line CPU(s) list: 0-1023 Vendor ID: AuthenticAMD Model name: AMD EPYC-Turin Processor CPU family: 26 Model: 0 Thread(s) per core: 2 Core(s) per socket: 256 Socket(s): 2 ... L1d cache: 24 MiB (512 instances) L1i cache: 16 MiB (512 instances) L2 cache: 512 MiB (512 instances) L3 cache: 64 MiB (2 instances) ... vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index1/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index2/shared_cpu_list 0-1 vm1:~ # cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index3/shared_cpu_list 0-511

And the topology, from inside each VM, will look as follows:
sect3.screen: vm1:~ # lscpu ... CPU(s): 512 On-line CPU(s) list: 0-511 Vendor ID: AuthenticAMD Model name: AMD EPYC-Turin Processor CPU family: 26 Model: 0 Thread(s) per core: 2 Core(s) per socket: 256 Socket(s): 1 ... L1d cache: 12 MiB (256 instances) L1i cache: 8 MiB (256 instances) L2 cache: 256 MiB (256 instances) L3 cache: 256 MiB (8 instances) ...

sect3.title: Dedicated vCPUs hint
sect3.para: When the vCPUs of a VM are pinned to physical CPUs which are not used by anything else (like in all the configurations described in this guide), the guest OS can be informed of that, with the following element of the VM configuration:

This is only a hint: it tells the guest OS that its vCPUs are never preempted for a long time, and the guest is then free to enable (or not) optimizations that are meaningful only in that case. It makes sense only if vCPUs are pinned 1-to-1 to dedicated pCPUs and, therefore, it should not be used when oversubscribing the host. It is also needed by some features of the guest, such as the cpuidle-haltpoll driver. All the experiments described in this guide were run with this hint enabled and we did not evaluate its specific impact on performance. See for a complete VM configuration file.

sect3.title: Memory backing
sect3.para: Memory wise, the VMs must be told to use the Huge Pages that were reserved for them. To effectively use 1 GiB huge pages, the amount of memory each VM is given must be a multiple of 1 GiB. Also, KSM should be disabled and we also must ensure that VMs' memory is never going to be swapped out. This is all achieved as follows:

To verify that the appropriate type of memory is being used by the VMs, one can check the content of /proc/meminfo, with the VMs running, and observe that all the pre-allocated Huge Pages are actually occupied.
sect3.screen: host:~ # cat /proc/meminfo | grep Huge AnonHugePages: 0 kB ShmemHugePages: 0 kB FileHugePages: 0 kB HugePages_Total: 1792 HugePages_Free: 0 HugePages_Rsvd: 0 HugePages_Surp: 0 Hugepagesize: 1048576 kB Hugetlb: 1879048192 kB

sect3.title: Ballooning
sect3.para: To get the full benefit of Huge Pages, memory ballooning must also be avoided. In fact, if the ballooning driver is not Huge Pages-aware, using ballooning would end up splitting the pages in fragments, neutering their (positive) performance impact. Making sure that memory ballooning is not used is done as follows:
That is, by specifying in the <currentMemory> the same value already used in the <memory> element (and never changing the memory size of the VM at runtime).

sect3.title: (Transparent) Huge Pages
sect3.para: If huge pages are used for allocating the VMs’ memory on the host, they can also be used inside the VMs, either explicitly, or via THP. Whether that helps performance is workload dependent. The analysis and the considerations made in the first part of the document about using (T)HP on bare metal, can also be applied here.

sect3.title: Automatic NUMA balancing
sect3.para: Similarly to THP, if the VM is NUMA-aware, NUMAB can be used inside of it to boost the performance of most NUMA-unaware workloads running inside the VM itself.

sect3.title: Services and daemons
sect3.para: irqbalance can be a source of latency inside of the VM, because of the way it uses the /proc/interrupts interface. For workloads that are particularly sensitive to latency, consider disabling it within the VMs (of course by taking the appropriate alternative measures, like binding IRQs, if necessary).

Managing Virtualization Platforms with libvirt: Installing an AMD SEV-SNP virtual machine

sect2.para: describe how to configure a VM to use AMD SEV-SNP (on an AMD SEV-SNP capable and properly configured host), which is not in the scope of this document. Refer to the linked materials for the details. The restrictions that apply to SEV-SNP VMs on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 are listed in Virtualization Support in SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (section AMD SEV-SNP confidential computing VM restrictions).
It is possible to check if the host is properly configured to run SEV-SNP VMs with the following command:
sect2.screen: dmesg | grep -i snp [ 0.000000] [ T0] SEV-SNP: RMP table physical range [0x00000201f6e00000 - 0x00000203faefffff] [ 0.004458] [ T0] SEV-SNP: Reserving start/end of RMP table on a 2MB boundary [0x00000203fae00000] [ 9.443247] [ T1] AMD-Vi: IOMMU SNP support enabled. [ 10.658851] [ T1] AMD-Vi: Extended features (0xa5bf732fa2285afe, 0x1f53f): PPR X2APIC NX GT [5] IA GA PC GA_vAPIC SNP [ 37.129870] [ T8005] ccp 0000:01:00.5: SEV-SNP API:1.59 build:3 [ 39.867334] [ T10811] kvm_amd: SEV-SNP enabled (ASIDs 1 - 99)
sect2.para: Once inside of the VM, this is how one can check whether both the memory and the VM state are encrypted, and the integrity of the VM is protected (with SEV-SNP):
sect2.screen: vm1:~ # dmesg | grep SEV [ 3.419580] [ T0] Memory Encryption Features active: AMD SEV SEV-ES SEV-SNP [ 3.423581] [ T0] SEV: Status: SEV SEV-ES SEV-SNP [ 3.689871] [ T1] SEV: APIC: wakeup_secondary_cpu() replaced with wakeup_cpu_via_vmgexit() [ 4.366601] [ T1] SEV: Using SNP CPUID table, 38 entries present. [ 4.366602] [ T1] SEV: SNP running at VMPL0. [ 4.509444] [ T1] SEV: SNP guest platform devices initialized. [ 6.893288] [ T1829] sev-guest sev-guest: Initialized SEV guest driver (using VMPCK0 communication key)
sect2.para: Note that it is not possible to provide a virtual IOMMU device to an encrypted VM. This means that, for having a functional SEV-SNP VM, we need to remove the iommu element, in the <devices> section of the VM configuration. And since that element is necessary for having more than 255 vCPUs in the VM, all the experiments conducted with SEV-SNP enabled have been done in VMs with at most 128 vCPUs.

Similarly, the memory of a SEV-SNP VM cannot be backed by the huge pages preallocated on the host via hugetlbfs, as described in . For this reason, all the SEV-SNP experiments presented in this document were run without them.

sect1.title: candidate workloads under a virtualization environment
sect1.para: Similarly to chapter we present two candidate workloads as examples of applications tuned for Zen6 in a variety of virtualized environments.

sect2.title: STREAM
sect2.para: The effectiveness of the proposed tuning is demonstrated using the STREAM benchmark.

sect3.title: Test scenario: One large VM
sect3.para: and show the bandwidth achieved by STREAM when the benchmark is built in single thread mode ('single') or parallelized with OpenMP ('openmp'), with as many threads as there are LLCs (16) in the former and with twice as many (32) in the latter. For both cases, we compare the results achieved on the host ('BM') and inside one VM ('VM').

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - Bare metal compared with one VM, with as many threads as LLCs
STREAM Bandwidth - Bare metal compared with one VM, with twice as many threads as LLCs

sect3.para: Both the single thread and the parallel results are very close between bare metal (blue and yellow rectangles) and inside of the VM (orange and green rectangles), for all the operations (Copy, Scale, Add and Triad) of the benchmark. The differences are small: below 5% in all cases.

This clearly shows how proper tuning allows a single VM running on an AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processor server to achieve a memory bandwidth that is comparable to the one that we can reach directly on the host.

note.para: Inside of the VM, the STREAM benchmark was configured almost identically to what has been shown already in .

sect3.para: and show the effect of using different CPU models for the virtual machine.

The OpenMP run in clearly shows some problems when the host-passthrough CPU model is selected. In fact, since using that model builds a VM with only 2 LLCs (and also because of the other problems with the cache topology), running STREAM with as many threads as there are LLCs in the system, or with twice as many, results in the benchmark spawning only 2 and 4 of them (orange and green rectangles, respectively). And this, of course, dramatically reduces the performance. With host-model, instead, the same two configurations result in 16 and 32 threads (blue and yellow rectangles) and in good performance. In , the blue and yellow rectangles are exactly the same as in the previous figure, while the orange and green ones show what happens if we instead manually set (via the configuration of the benchmark) the number of threads to 16 and 32, that is the same values used with host-model. In this case, performance is restored to how good we know things can be from and (and from the host-model results, see the blue and yellow rectangles).

It is also interesting to note that with host-passthrough and 32 threads (green rectangles) we reach slightly better performance than with host-model (yellow rectangles), while with 16 threads the results are the same (orange and blue rectangles). However, this is not worth the inconvenience of not being able to rely on the topology of the VM, and on parameters like the number of LLCs, that it is perfectly reasonable to expect to be able to count on. This means that it is fine to stick with host-model, and it is not worthwhile setting host-passthrough and coping manually with the misconfigured cache hierarchy inside of the VM (as that could potentially be much more complicated than it has been here for the STREAM benchmark or, sometimes, even impossible).

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP in one VM with different CPU models
STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP in one VM with different CPU models and the same number of threads

sect3.para: This situation also confirms the need to always run benchmarks for assessing the performance of the relevant workloads, on a given platform. In fact, because of specific characteristics of some components of the virtualization stack available in SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 the EPYC-Turin (or, equivalently, the host-model) CPU model might be preferable to what it would have appeared to be the most obvious choice (host-passthrough).

sect3.title: Test scenario: Multiple VMs
sect3.para: and show what happens when 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 VMs are used. The former reports the average bandwidth achieved in each experiment, considering all the VMs involved. For example, the yellow bar (4 VMs) is relative to an experiment where 4 VMs were concurrently running the STREAM benchmark (in single thread mode) and represents the average of the 4 different memory bandwidth values, one for each of such VMs. The latter shows something similar, but the bars represent the cumulative STREAM bandwidth achieved in each experiment, considering all the VMs involved. For example, the light blue bar (32 VMs) is relative to an experiment where 32 VMs were concurrently running the STREAM benchmark (in single thread mode) and represents the sum of the 32 different memory bandwidth values, one for each of such VMs.

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - Single, average of the bandwidth achieved among all VMs of each group
STREAM Bandwidth - Single, sum of the bandwidth achieved within all VMs of each group

sect3.para: We see in how the single STREAM bandwidth is basically constant up to 4 VMs, suffers a bit of a decline with 8 and 16 VMs and a much more significant one with 32 and 64 VMs, as more VMs are packed on the NUMA nodes and, hence, compete for the bandwidth of the memory controllers. However, reminds us how the total bandwidth achieved, if we consider all the VMs involved in each experiment, actually goes up (and it scales roughly linearly up to 16 VMs), until it saturates when 32 and 64 VMs are used.

and show the same, but when the parallel (via OpenMP) version of STREAM is run, inside of each VM of each experiment, with as many threads as there are LLCs in the VM. and show the same again, but with twice as many threads as there are LLCs. Note that the number of LLCs (and, hence, of threads) depends on the topology of the VMs and it is, therefore, not always the same. For example, it is 16 for the one big VM, and 1 for the VMs that use one die or less.

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP (as many threads as LLCs), average of the bandwidth achieved among all VMs of each group
STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP (as many threads as LLCs), sum of the bandwidth achieved within all VMs of each group
STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP (twice as many threads as LLCs), average of the bandwidth achieved among all VMs of each group
STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP (twice as many threads as LLCs), sum of the bandwidth achieved within all VMs of each group

sect3.para: In and we see that performance scales down in a close to linear fashion with the increase of the number of VMs involved, up to 16 VMs (the bandwidth achieved in each VM is halved every time the number of VMs doubles), and less than linearly with 32 and 64 VMs. At the same time, and show how the total cumulative bandwidth of each experiment stays pretty much constant up to 16 VMs, as one would expect, since the total number of threads running STREAM is the same in all these experiments. With 32 and 64 VMs, instead, each VM still has only one LLC, and the total number of threads (and, hence, the bandwidth requested to the memory controllers) increases accordingly. As a consequence, the total bandwidth goes up as well, although with twice as many threads as LLCs it saturates for some of the STREAM operations when going from 32 to 64 VMs (for example, Scale). Actually, for some of the STREAM operations it even seems that using many small VMs may make it possible to exploit even better (as compared to what happens when one large VM is running, even with the same total number of threads) the large memory bandwidth provided by the memory controllers of the AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processors.

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - One VM compared with many VMs, with the same total number of threads

sect3.para: shows this, by comparing the total bandwidth achieved with many VMs against the one achieved by a single VM, running STREAM with the same total number of threads (the labels on top of the bars tell how many VMs were involved). It confirms that the number of threads is what matters the most: one VM reaches its top bandwidth with 64 to 128 threads and gains nothing from using even more of them (with 256 threads the results are about the same and, with 512 threads and more, Copy even drops to about 1140 GB/s). It also shows that, with the same number of threads, many VMs do slightly better than one (by up to 12%). And, with 128 threads in total (64 VMs, with two threads each), Copy and Triad go beyond what one VM can reach, no matter how many threads it uses (by 19% and 14%, respectively). For Scale and Add, instead, the maximum is the same.

sect3.title: Test scenario: Secure Nested Paging
sect3.para: The goal for this test was evaluating the impact on the performance of encrypting the VMs with SEV-SNP, when running a memory intensive workload like STREAM. Since SEV-SNP VMs cannot use preallocated huge pages, the VMs were run without them, both with and without SEV-SNP, in order to have a fair comparison. The absolute values are, therefore, not comparable with the ones from the previous sections.

Considering the case when 8 VMs are concurrently running on the host and are executing the STREAM benchmark, shows the average bandwidth of the single thread execution of the benchmark in all such VMs when memory is not encrypted (blue bars) and when the VMs are encrypted with SEV-SNP (orange bars). shows the same for the OpenMP version of the benchmark, with as many threads as there are LLCs in each VM (2) and with twice as many (4): the blue and orange bars are, respectively, the VMs that are not encrypted and the ones that are encrypted in the first case, the yellow and green bars in the second.

figure.title: STREAM Bandwidth - Single, average bandwidth in 8 VMs when unencrypted, encrypted with SEV-SNP
STREAM Bandwidth - OpenMP (LLCs and 2xLLCs threads), average bandwidth in 8 VMs when unencrypted, encrypted with SEV-SNP

sect3.para: It is quite evident how SEV-SNP has a close to nonexistent impact on the performance for this workload (the difference is at most 1% in the single thread case and at most 3% in the OpenMP one). Actually, it may even seem that encrypted VMs are slightly faster, but we should note how, at least in the OpenMP case, all the differences fall within the error bars.

sect2.title: NASA Parallel Benchmark
sect2.para: Trying to match the experimental evaluation done on bare-metal, NPB base workloads have also been considered.

sect3.title: Test scenario: One large VM
sect3.para: shows the results of running the various NPB workloads on the host and in one VM. In both cases, the tuning introduced above was applied (in the latter case, of course, inside of the VM itself).

figure.title: NAS Completion Time - bare metal and in one VM

sect3.para: Like for the STREAM case, a properly tuned VM can reach pretty much the same performance as the host (the differences are within 5%, with the exception of ep.D, which runs for only a few seconds).
shows again the impact on the performance of different CPU models.

figure.title: NAS Completion Time - One VM with different CPU models

sect3.para: host-passthrough is faster than host-model for some of the benchmarks, by up to 30% (is.D), 16% (mg.D), 13% (cg.D), 12% (ep.D) and, only slightly, 7% (sp.D), while the results for the other ones are the same. Notice that the largest differences are for the benchmarks that run for only a few seconds. Therefore, as already said for STREAM, considering that host-model runs show good results in all cases, this guide recommends using it and avoiding the potential issues coming from having an inaccurate topology and a misleading cache hierarchy representation inside of VMs.

sect3.title: Test scenario: Two to sixty-four VMs
sect3.para: depicts the same as , but for a few more cases, in terms of number of concurrently running VMs (note that the vertical axis has a logarithmic scale).

figure.title: NAS Completion Time - bare metal and 1 to 64 VMs

sect3.para: We can see how the slowdown is linear (and for most of the benchmarks even sub-linear) with the number of the VMs (the only exceptions being sp.D, from 4 VMs on, and lu.D with 32 and 64 VMs). And that makes sense considering that when we increase the number of VMs, each one of them can also have fewer CPUs. This testifies the effectiveness of the suggested tuning measures, when it comes to guarantee a good level of isolation among multiple concurrently running VMs on the AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processors. Notice that mg.D could not be run with 64 VMs, because of the small amount of RAM that each VM has in that case, and that sp.D was not run.

sect3.title: Test scenario: Eight VMs with Secure Nested Paging
sect3.para: Similarly to what has been done with STREAM, we evaluate here the overhead introduced by SEV-SNP, this time for CPU-bound workloads, and we do that by running the NPB benchmarks inside eight VMs concurrently that are all either unencrypted or encrypted with SEV-SNP (). As for STREAM, the VMs were run without preallocated huge pages in both cases.

figure.title: NAS Completion Time - Tuned configuration in 8 VMs, with and without SEV-SNP

sect3.para: As for the memory-intensive case, the overhead introduced by the Confidential Computing technology is found to be really close to zero: the difference between the unencrypted and the encrypted VMs is at most 2%, well within the variability among the VMs.

sect1.title: Conclusion
sect1.para: The introduction of the AMD EPYC 9006 Series Processors continues to push the boundaries of what is possible for memory and I/O-bound workloads with significantly higher bandwidth and an increased number of channels. A properly configured and tuned workload can exceed the performance of many contemporary off-the-shelf solutions even when fully customized. The symmetric and balanced nature of the machine makes the task of tuning a workload considerably easier, given that each partition can have symmetric performance. And this is a property that can turn out particularly handy in virtualization, as each virtual machine can be assigned to each one of the partitions.

With SUSE Linux Enterprise 16.1, all the tools to monitor and tune a workload are readily available. You can extract the maximum performance and reliability running your applications on the 6th Generation AMD EPYC Processor platform.
